Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether the non-measurability of a single preimage $g^{-1}(a,b)$ implies $g$ is not measurable.

## Proof

**Definition.** A function $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is (Lebesgue) measurable if $g^{-1}((c, \infty))$ is a measurable set for every $c \in \mathbb{R}$.

**Key equivalence.** We first establish that the following are equivalent:
1. $g$ is measurable (i.e., $g^{-1}((c,\infty))$ is measurable for all $c$).
2. $g^{-1}((a,b))$ is measurable for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

**(1) $\Rightarrow$ (2):** Suppose $g$ is measurable. For any $a < b$:
$$g^{-1}((a,b)) = g^{-1}((a,\infty)) \cap g^{-1}((-\infty,b)).$$
The set $g^{-1}((a,\infty))$ is measurable by hypothesis. For $g^{-1}((-\infty,b))$, note:
$$g^{-1}((-\infty,b)) = \mathbb{R} \setminus g^{-1}([b,\infty)),$$
and
$$g^{-1}([b,\infty)) = \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} g^{-1}\!\left(\left(b - \tfrac{1}{n},\, \infty\right)\right),$$
which is a countable intersection of measurable sets, hence measurable. Therefore $g^{-1}((-\infty,b))$ is measurable, and so $g^{-1}((a,b))$ is the intersection of two measurable sets, hence measurable. (The cases $a \geq b$ give $\emptyset$, trivially measurable.)

**(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1):** Suppose $g^{-1}((a,b))$ is measurable for all $a, b$. For any $c \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$g^{-1}((c,\infty)) = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} g^{-1}((c,\, c+n)),$$
which is a countable union of measurable sets, hence measurable. So $g$ is measurable. $\square$

**Main argument.** The equivalence above states:
$$g \text{ is measurable} \iff \forall\, a, b \in \mathbb{R},\; g^{-1}((a,b)) \text{ is measurable}.$$

Taking the contrapositive:
$$\exists\, a, b \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } g^{-1}((a,b)) \text{ is not measurable} \iff g \text{ is not measurable}.$$

Therefore, if $g^{-1}((a,b))$ is not measurable for some $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$, we **can** conclude that $g$ is not measurable. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
